exercise1.prompt: numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], print the first, the last with a negative index, and the middle

hiddenCases.name: the first, then the last, then the middle
nothing was added to or taken out of the list

exercise1.hint: Indexes start at 0, so the first item is not numbers[1] and the fifth is not numbers[5]. A negative index counts back from the end, which saves you working out the length.

exercise2.prompt: letters = ["a".."f"], print the first three, the last two, and items 2 through 4
exercise2.hint: The number after the colon says where to stop, and the slice stops before it. So a slice that should end at index 4 is written with a 5.

questions.explain: A negative index counts back from the end, and -1 is the last item. It is shorter and safer than numbers[len(numbers) - 1].
A slice starts at the first number and stops before the second, so 1:3 gives you indexes 1 and 2 and never index 3.

questions.prompt: For letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"], match each slice to what it gives.
questions.explain: A missing start means the beginning and a missing stop means the end, so [:] is the whole list -- and a fresh copy of it.

questions.prompt: numbers[5] on a list of five items raises an ___ error, because the last index is 4.
questions.explain: Counting from 0 means the highest valid index is always one less than the length. Slices are forgiving about running past the end; plain indexing is not.
